section.title: oosqlBackupFinish
section.para: Called to release all resources associated with the backup operation. This function is part of the support for the online backup feature of SQLite.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
buHandle [required]
The non-null handle to the backup returned from oosqlBackupInit.

Returns .ooSQLite~OK if no errors occurred during a call to oosqlBackupStep, whether or not the backup operation completed. If an out-of-memory condition or IO error occurred during any prior call of oosqlBackupStep using the buHandle argument, then oosqlBackupFinish returns the corresponding error code.

There should be exactly one call to oosqlBackupFinish for each successful call of oosqlBackupInit. Once oosqlBackupFinish has been called, buHandle is no longer valid and must not be used in any other call to a function.
The functionality of the oosqlBackupFinish routine is similar to that of the sqlite3_backup_finish SQLite API

This example shows part of the code that performs an online backup of a very large database which is concurrently in heavy use. If the backup does not finish in four hours, the application abandons the backup and reschedules it to a different time:
-- This function will return DONE if completed and BUSY if abandoned. Any other -- return would be a fatal error. ::routine backupWithTimeLimit use strict arg buHandle, limit
count = 0 do while .true ret = oosqlBackupStep(buHandle, 2) if ret == .ooSQLite~DONE then do say 'Backup finished with no error.' outcome = .ooSQLite~DONE leave end
if ret <> .ooSQLite~OK, ret <> .ooSQLite~BUSY, ret <> .ooSQLite~LOCKED then do say 'Fatal error during back up.' outcome = ret leave end
if count * 2 > limit then do say say "Backup has not completed within the time limit, going to abandon the operation." say outcome = .ooSQLite~BUSY leave end
j = SysSleep(.5) count += 1
end
ret = oosqlBackupFinish(buHandle)
return outcome

section.title: oosqlBackupInit
section.para: Called once to initialize an online backup. This function is part of the support for the online backup feature of SQLite.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
dstConn [required]
An open database connection. This database is used as the destination of the backup.
srcConn [required]
An open database connection. This database is used as the source of the backup.
dstName [optional]
The name of the destination backup. This is not the file name but rather the main, temp, or attached as name. If omitted, main is used.
srcName [optional]
The name of the source backup. Again, this is not the file name but rather the main, temp, or attached as name. If omitted, main is used.
Returns a handle that is used in the calls to other functions that are part of the online backup feature. This handle may be null if an error ocurred. See the remarks for a discussion on this.

If an error occurs within the call to oosqlBackupInit, then the handle returned will be null. Use the oosqlIsHandleNull routine to check for this. On error, an error code and error message are stored in the destination database connection. This error code and message can be retrieved using the oosqlErrCode and oosqlErrMsg functions A successful call to oosqlBackupInit returns a non-null handle. The handle may be used with the oosqlBackupStep and oosqlBackupFinish, functions to perform the specified backup operation. The non-null handle is also used in the oosqlBackupPageCount and oosqlBackupRemaining functions.
The functionality of the oosqlBackupInit routine is similar to that of the sqlite3_backup_init SQLite API

This example initializes a backup and checks for error:
buHandle = oosqlBackupInit(destDB, srcDB) if oosqlIsHandleNull(buHandle) then do say 'Error initializing backup. Error code:' oosqlErrCode(destDB) oosqlErrMsg(destDB) r = oosqlClose(srcDB) r = oosqlClose(destDB) return 99. end

section.title: oosqlBackupPageCount
section.para: Returns the total number of pages in the source database file. This function is part of the support for the online backup feature of SQLite.

listitem.para:
The single argument is:
buHandle [required]
The non-null handle to the backup returned from oosqlBackupInit.
The total number of pages in the source database file.
The functionality of the oosqlBackupPageCount routine is similar to that of the sqlite3_backup_pagecount SQLite API.

section.title: oosqlBackupRemaining
section.para: Returns the number of pages still to be backed up in the source database file. This function is part of the support for the online backup feature of SQLite.

listitem.para:
The single argument is:
buHandle [required]
The non-null handle to the backup returned from oosqlBackupInit.
The number of pages in the source database file that still need to be backed up.
The functionality of the oosqlBackupRemaining routine is similar to that of the sqlite3_backup_remaining SQLite API .

This example shows how to calculate the percentage complete of a backup. The code snippet would be executed after a call to oosqlBackupStep(). Maybe every call, or every 5th call, ...
remain = oosqlBackupRemaining(buHandle) pages = oosqlBackupPageCount(buHandle)
percentComplete = 100 * (pages - remain) / pages
say "Backup" percentComplete "percent complete..."
/* Output might be:
Backup 8 percent complete... Backup 16 percent complete... Backup 24 percent complete... Backup 32 percent complete... Backup 40 percent complete... Backup 48 percent complete...
*/

section.title: oosqlBackupStep
section.para: Copies up to count pages between the source and destination databases specified by the buHandle argument. This function is part of the support for the online backup feature of SQLite.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
buHandle [required]
The non-null handle to the backup returned from oosqlBackupInit.
count
The whole number count of database pages to copy. If count is negative, all of the remaining pages are copied. If count is omitted it defaults to 5.

If count pages are successfully copied, and there are still more pages to be copied, then OK (.ooSQLite~OK) is returned. If oosqlBackupStep successfully finishes copying all pages from source to destination, then DONE (.ooSQLite~DONE) is returned. Otherwise an error code is returned. Some errors are fatal and some are not. The remarks section further discusses this.

If the database engine can not obtain a required lock then oosqlBackupStep returns BUSY (.ooSQLite~BUSY.) If the source database connection is being used to write to the source database when oosqlBackupStep is called, then LOCKED is returned. The return code can also be NOMEM, READONLY, or one of the IO_ERR_XXX codes. After BUSY or LOCKED, oosqlBackupStep can be tried again. But NOMEM, READONLY, and IO_ERR_XXX are considered fatal. There is no point in retrying if any of those codes are returned. The application must accept that the backup operation has failed and call finish to release associated resources.
The functionality of the oosqlStep routine is similar to that of the sqlite3_backup_step SQLite API.

This example initializes a backup, copies everything in one step, checks for error, and cleans up:
...
buObj = oosqlBackupInit(srcConn, dstConn)
if oosqlIsHandleNull(buObj) then do -- handle error ... end
ret = oosqlBackupStep(buObj, -1)
if ret \== .ooSQLite~DONE then do -- back up failed, handle error ret = oosqlBackupFinish(buObj) ... end
-- Backup okay, we are done with the connections -- and the backup handle, close everything ... ret = oosqlBackupFinish(buObj) ret = oosqlClose(dstConn) ret = oosqlClose(srcConn)
return 0

section.title: oosqlBindBlob
section.para: Binds a BLOB value to a host parameter of a prepared statement.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
stmt [required]
The handle to a statement prepared by oosqlPrepare. The handle must not be null, and the statement must not have been finalized: see the rules for statement handles.
index [required]
The index of the host parameter, 1 for the first parameter. The index of a named parameter can be obtained with oosqlBindParameterIndex.
value [required]
The data to bind: a String, a Buffer, or a MutableBuffer object. All the bytes of the data are bound, including any embedded NUL characters.
Returns OK on success, or one of the Result Code constants on error: RANGE if index is not the index of a parameter of the statement, MISUSE if the statement has been stepped and not reset.

The data is copied by SQLite, so the object passed as value can be changed after the routine returns. What is said here about binding values applies to all the oosqlBind routines: values can only be bound before the statement is first stepped, or after it is reset; a bound value stays in place, also after a reset, until another value is bound to the same parameter, or the bindings are cleared with oosqlClearBindings; and a parameter that has not been bound is NULL.
Raises a syntax error, 88.900, if value is not a String, a Buffer, or a MutableBuffer.
The functionality of the oosqlBindBlob routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_bind_blob API.
The bindBlob method of the ooSQLiteStmt class does the same for a statement object.

This example stores some binary data in the picture column of a row:
picture = 'FFD8FFE0'x || 'not really a JPEG image' rc = oosqlPrepare(db, "UPDATE foods SET picture = ? WHERE name = 'Bacon';", 'stmt') rc = oosqlBindBlob(stmt, 1, picture) if rc == .ooSQLite~OK then rc = oosqlStep(stmt) if rc <> .ooSQLite~DONE then say 'Error:' oosqlErrMsg(db) call oosqlFinalize stmt

section.title: oosqlBindDouble
section.para: Binds a floating point value to a host parameter of a prepared statement.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
stmt [required]
The handle to a statement prepared by oosqlPrepare. The handle must not be null, and the statement must not have been finalized: see the rules for statement handles.
index [required]
The index of the host parameter, 1 for the first parameter.
value [required]
The number to bind. It is converted to a double precision floating point number.
Returns OK on success, or one of the Result Code constants on error, as oosqlBindBlob does.
See the remarks of oosqlBindBlob for when values can be bound, and how long they stay bound. The example of oosqlBindNull also uses oosqlBindDouble.
Raises a syntax error if value is not a number.
The functionality of the oosqlBindDouble routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_bind_double API.
The bindDouble method of the ooSQLiteStmt class does the same for a statement object.

section.title: oosqlBindInt
section.para: Binds a 32-bit integer value to a host parameter of a prepared statement.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
stmt [required]
The handle to a statement prepared by oosqlPrepare. The handle must not be null, and the statement must not have been finalized: see the rules for statement handles.
index [required]
The index of the host parameter, 1 for the first parameter.
value [required]
The whole number to bind, which must fit in 32 bits: from -2147483648 to 2147483647. Use oosqlBindInt64 for larger numbers.
Returns OK on success, or one of the Result Code constants on error, as oosqlBindBlob does.
See the remarks of oosqlBindBlob for when values can be bound, and how long they stay bound. The examples of oosqlBindNull and oosqlReset also use oosqlBindInt.
Raises a syntax error if value is not a whole number that fits in 32 bits.
The functionality of the oosqlBindInt routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_bind_int API.
The bindInt method of the ooSQLiteStmt class does the same for a statement object.

section.title: oosqlBindInt64
section.para: Binds a 64-bit integer value to a host parameter of a prepared statement.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
stmt [required]
The handle to a statement prepared by oosqlPrepare. The handle must not be null, and the statement must not have been finalized: see the rules for statement handles.
index [required]
The index of the host parameter, 1 for the first parameter.
value [required]
The whole number to bind, which must fit in 64 bits: from -9223372036854775808 to 9223372036854775807.
Returns OK on success, or one of the Result Code constants on error, as oosqlBindBlob does.
See the remarks of oosqlBindBlob for when values can be bound, and how long they stay bound.
Raises a syntax error if value is not a whole number that fits in 64 bits.
The functionality of the oosqlBindInt64 routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_bind_int64 API.
The bindInt64 method of the ooSQLiteStmt class does the same for a statement object.

This example stores a number that does not fit in 32 bits:
rc = oosqlExec(db, "CREATE TABLE counters(name TEXT, value INTEGER);") rc = oosqlPrepare(db, "INSERT INTO counters VALUES('bytes', ?);", 'stmt') rc = oosqlBindInt64(stmt, 1, 9876543210) rc = oosqlStep(stmt) call oosqlFinalize stmt

section.title: oosqlBindNull
section.para: Binds the SQL NULL value to a host parameter of a prepared statement.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
stmt [required]
The handle to a statement prepared by oosqlPrepare. The handle must not be null, and the statement must not have been finalized: see the rules for statement handles.
index [required]
The index of the host parameter, 1 for the first parameter.
Returns OK on success, or one of the Result Code constants on error, as oosqlBindBlob does.
A parameter that has never been bound is already NULL. oosqlBindNull is needed to set to NULL a parameter that was bound to another value; oosqlClearBindings does it for all the parameters at once.
The functionality of the oosqlBindNull routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_bind_null API.
The bindNull method of the ooSQLiteStmt class does the same for a statement object.

This example inserts two rows with the same statement. The second one has no price:
sql = "INSERT INTO foods(type_id, name, price) VALUES(?, ?, ?);" rc = oosqlPrepare(db, sql, 'stmt')
rc = oosqlBindInt(stmt, 1, 2) rc = oosqlBindText(stmt, 2, 'Ham') rc = oosqlBindDouble(stmt, 3, 4.5) rc = oosqlStep(stmt)
rc = oosqlReset(stmt) rc = oosqlBindInt(stmt, 1, 3) rc = oosqlBindText(stmt, 2, 'Brie') rc = oosqlBindNull(stmt, 3) -- no price yet rc = oosqlStep(stmt)
call oosqlFinalize stmt

section.title: oosqlBindParameterCount
section.para: Returns the number of host parameters in a prepared statement.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
stmt [required]
The handle to a statement prepared by oosqlPrepare. The handle must not be null, and the statement must not have been finalized: see the rules for statement handles.
The index of the last host parameter of the statement, or 0 if it has none.

This is the number of parameters when the parameters are written as ?, or as names: :name, @name, or $name. A named parameter that appears more than once in the SQL is a single parameter. When the parameters are numbered explicitly, as in ?NNN, the numbers can leave gaps, and the value returned is the largest number used, not the number of parameters.
The functionality of the oosqlBindParameterCount routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_bind_parameter_count API.
The bindParameterCount method of the ooSQLiteStmt class does the same for a statement object.
See the example of oosqlBindParameterIndex.

section.title: oosqlBindParameterIndex
section.para: Returns the index of the host parameter with the given name.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
stmt [required]
The handle to a statement prepared by oosqlPrepare. The handle must not be null, and the statement must not have been finalized: see the rules for statement handles.
name [required]
The name of the parameter, as written in the SQL, including its first character: for the parameter :type, the name is :type, not type. The comparison is case sensitive.
The index of the parameter, which can be used with the oosqlBind routines, or 0 if the statement has no parameter with that name.
The functionality of the oosqlBindParameterIndex routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_bind_parameter_index API.
The bindParameterIndex method of the ooSQLiteStmt class does the same for a statement object.

This example lists the parameters of a statement, binds them by name, and executes it:
sql = "SELECT name FROM foods WHERE type_id = :type AND price < :maxPrice;" rc = oosqlPrepare(db, sql, 'stmt')
do i = 1 to oosqlBindParameterCount(stmt) say i oosqlBindParameterName(stmt, i) end
rc = oosqlBindInt(stmt, oosqlBindParameterIndex(stmt, ':type'), 1) rc = oosqlBindDouble(stmt, oosqlBindParameterIndex(stmt, ':maxPrice'), 1.4) do while oosqlStep(stmt) == .ooSQLite~ROW say oosqlColumnText(stmt, 1) end call oosqlFinalize stmt
/* Output:
1 :type 2 :maxPrice Bagels */

section.title: oosqlBindParameterName
section.para: Returns the name of the host parameter with the given index.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
stmt [required]
The handle to a statement prepared by oosqlPrepare. The handle must not be null, and the statement must not have been finalized: see the rules for statement handles.
index [required]
The index of the host parameter, 1 for the first parameter.

The name of the parameter as written in the SQL, including its first character, such as :type. For a parameter written as ?, which has no name, and for an index that is out of range, the empty string is returned. A parameter written as ?NNN has that text as its name.
The functionality of the oosqlBindParameterName routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_bind_parameter_name API.
The bindParameterName method of the ooSQLiteStmt class does the same for a statement object.
See the example of oosqlBindParameterIndex.

section.title: oosqlBindText
section.para: Binds a text value to a host parameter of a prepared statement.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
stmt [required]
The handle to a statement prepared by oosqlPrepare. The handle must not be null, and the statement must not have been finalized: see the rules for statement handles.
index [required]
The index of the host parameter, 1 for the first parameter.
text [required]
The string to bind. SQLite expects the text to be UTF-8. The text ends at its first NUL character, if it has one: use oosqlBindBlob for data that can contain NUL characters.
Returns OK on success, or one of the Result Code constants on error, as oosqlBindBlob does.
The text is copied by SQLite. See the remarks of oosqlBindBlob for when values can be bound, and how long they stay bound. The example of oosqlBindNull also uses oosqlBindText.
The functionality of the oosqlBindText routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_bind_text API.
The bindText method of the ooSQLiteStmt class does the same for a statement object.

section.title: oosqlBindValue
section.para: Binds a value taken from a result column of a statement to a host parameter of a prepared statement. The value keeps its datatype: an integer is bound as an integer, a BLOB as a BLOB, and so on.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
stmt [required]
The handle to a statement prepared by oosqlPrepare. The handle must not be null, and the statement must not have been finalized: see the rules for statement handles.
index [required]
The index of the host parameter, 1 for the first parameter.
value [required]
A value returned by oosqlColumnValue, which is a Pointer object.
Returns OK on success, or one of the Result Code constants on error, as oosqlBindBlob does.

The value returned by oosqlColumnValue is only valid while the statement it comes from stays on the same result row: it must be bound before that statement is stepped again, reset, or finalized. Once it is bound, SQLite has its own copy. Passing any other Pointer, or a value that is no longer valid, has unpredictable results, and can crash the interpreter.
Raises a syntax error if value is not a Pointer object.
The functionality of the oosqlBindValue routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_bind_value API.
The bindValue method of the ooSQLiteStmt class does the same for a statement object.

This example copies some rows from one table to another, keeping the datatypes of the values:
rc = oosqlExec(db, "CREATE TABLE cheap(name TEXT, price REAL);") rc = oosqlPrepare(db, "SELECT name, price FROM foods WHERE price < 2;", 'src') rc = oosqlPrepare(db, "INSERT INTO cheap VALUES(?, ?);", 'dst')
do while oosqlStep(src) == .ooSQLite~ROW rc = oosqlBindValue(dst, 1, oosqlColumnValue(src, 1)) rc = oosqlBindValue(dst, 2, oosqlColumnValue(src, 2)) rc = oosqlStep(dst) rc = oosqlReset(dst) end
call oosqlFinalize src call oosqlFinalize dst

section.title: oosqlBindZeroBlob
section.para: Binds a BLOB filled with zeros to a host parameter of a prepared statement.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
stmt [required]
The handle to a statement prepared by oosqlPrepare. The handle must not be null, and the statement must not have been finalized: see the rules for statement handles.
index [required]
The index of the host parameter, 1 for the first parameter.
length [required]
The size of the BLOB, in bytes. A negative length is the same as 0.
Returns OK on success, or one of the Result Code constants on error, as oosqlBindBlob does.
SQLite does not use memory for the zeros while the statement runs, so this is an efficient way to reserve space for a large BLOB.
The functionality of the oosqlBindZeroBlob routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_bind_zeroblob API.
The bindZeroBlob method of the ooSQLiteStmt class does the same for a statement object.

This example sets the picture column of a row to 4096 zero bytes:
rc = oosqlPrepare(db, "UPDATE foods SET picture = ? WHERE name = 'Cheese';", 'stmt') rc = oosqlBindZeroBlob(stmt, 1, 4096) rc = oosqlStep(stmt) call oosqlFinalize stmt

section.title: oosqlBusyHandler
section.para: Registers a routine that is called when a table needed by a statement is locked by another connection.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
db [required]
The handle to a database connection, as set by oosqlOpen. The handle must not be null.
rtnName [required]
The name of the public routine to call when a table is locked, or the empty string to remove the routine registered before. See the rules for callback routines.
userData [optional]
Any object, passed to the routine as its second argument. If it is omitted, the routine receives .nil.
Returns OK on success, or one of the Result Code constants on error.

The routine is called with two arguments: the number of times it has already been called for this lock, 0 the first time, and the user data. It must return a whole number: not 0 to make SQLite try again, or 0 to give up, and then the statement returns BUSY. The routine usually waits a little before returning, with SysSleep for example.
There can be only one busy handler for a connection: oosqlBusyTimeOut replaces this one, and the other way round.
The functionality of the oosqlBusyHandler routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_busy_handler API.
The busyHandler method of the ooSQLiteConnection class does the same with a method of an object; see also busyCallBack.

This example locks the database with a second connection, and then shows how the busy handler of the first one is called before the statement returns BUSY:
rc = oosqlOpen(oosqlDbFileName(db, 'main'), 'other') rc = oosqlExec(other, "BEGIN EXCLUSIVE;") -- other connection locks the database
rc = oosqlBusyHandler(db, 'retry3Times') say oosqlExec(db, "SELECT count(*) FROM foods;") rc = oosqlBusyHandler(db, '')
rc = oosqlExec(other, "COMMIT;") rc = oosqlClose(other) /* Output: Waiting... 0 Waiting... 1 Waiting... 2 SQLite Error: rc = 5, database is locked */
::routine retry3Times public use arg count say 'Waiting...' count if count < 2 then do call SysSleep 0.1 return 1 -- try again end return 0 -- give up: BUSY

section.title: oosqlBusyTimeOut
section.para: Sets a busy handler that waits, for up to the given time, while a table is locked.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
db [required]
The handle to a database connection, as set by oosqlOpen. The handle must not be null, and the connection must not have been closed: see oosqlClose.
ms [required]
The number of milliseconds to wait. A value of 0 or less removes any busy handler.
Returns OK.

When a statement finds a table locked by another connection, the handler sleeps and retries, several times, until the lock is released or the total time has passed; then the statement returns BUSY. There can be only one busy handler for a connection: oosqlBusyTimeOut replaces a handler set with oosqlBusyHandler, and the other way round. By default there is no busy handler, and a statement returns BUSY at once.
The functionality of the oosqlBusyTimeOut routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_busy_timeout API.
The busyTimeOut method of the ooSQLiteConnection class does the same for a connection object.

This example makes the statements of a connection wait up to 3 seconds for a lock:
rc = oosqlBusyTimeOut(db, 3000) -- wait up to 3 seconds for a lock

section.title: oosqlChanges
section.para: Returns the number of rows changed, inserted, or deleted by the most recent INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE statement completed on a database connection.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
db [required]
The handle to a database connection, as set by oosqlOpen. The handle must not be null, and the connection must not have been closed: see oosqlClose.
The number of rows.

Only the changes made directly by the statement are counted, not those made by triggers or foreign key actions. Statements that are not an INSERT, an UPDATE, or a DELETE do not change the value. oosqlTotalChanges counts all the changes since the connection was opened.
The functionality of the oosqlChanges routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_changes API.
The changes method of the ooSQLiteConnection class does the same for a connection object.

This example shows the values of oosqlChanges and oosqlTotalChanges after two statements:
rc = oosqlExec(db, "UPDATE foods SET price = price * 1.1 WHERE type_id = 1;") say oosqlChanges(db) oosqlTotalChanges(db) -- 2 2 rc = oosqlExec(db, "DELETE FROM foods WHERE price IS NULL;") say oosqlChanges(db) oosqlTotalChanges(db) -- 1 3

section.title: oosqlClearBindings
section.para: Sets all the host parameters of a prepared statement to NULL.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
stmt [required]
The handle to a statement prepared by oosqlPrepare. The handle must not be null, and the statement must not have been finalized: see the rules for statement handles.
Returns OK.
oosqlReset does not change the values bound to the parameters. Use oosqlClearBindings when the next execution of the statement should not use them.
The functionality of the oosqlClearBindings routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_clear_bindings API.
The clearBindings method of the ooSQLiteStmt class does the same for a statement object.

In this example, the second row inserted gets NULL for the type and the price:
rc = oosqlPrepare(db, "INSERT INTO foods(type_id, name, price) VALUES(?, ?, ?);", 'stmt') rc = oosqlBindInt(stmt, 1, 2) rc = oosqlBindText(stmt, 2, 'Sausage') rc = oosqlBindDouble(stmt, 3, 2.25) rc = oosqlStep(stmt)
rc = oosqlReset(stmt) rc = oosqlClearBindings(stmt) -- type_id and price are now NULL rc = oosqlBindText(stmt, 2, 'Unknown food') rc = oosqlStep(stmt) call oosqlFinalize stmt

section.title: oosqlClose
section.para: Closes a database connection and releases the resources it uses.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
db [required]
The handle to a database connection, as set by oosqlOpen. The handle must not be null, and the connection must not have been closed: see oosqlClose.
Returns OK if the connection is closed, or BUSY if it has prepared statements that are not finalized, or backups that are not finished. In that case the connection stays open, and can still be used.

Every connection set by oosqlOpen must be closed, also when oosqlOpen returned an error. Before closing it, finalize its statements with oosqlFinalize (oosqlNextStmt finds them), and finish its backups with oosqlBackupFinish.

Once a connection has been closed, its handle is not valid any more, but it is not null: ooSQLite can not detect that it has been closed, and using it in any routine, also in oosqlClose, has unpredictable results, and can crash the interpreter. The object orientated interface does not have this problem: closing an ooSQLiteConnection object that is already closed does nothing.
The functionality of the oosqlClose routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_close API.
The close method of the ooSQLiteConnection class does the same for a connection object.

This example tries to close a connection that has a statement that is not finalized, and closes it after finalizing the statement:
rc = oosqlPrepare(db, "SELECT name FROM foods;", 'stmt') rc = oosqlClose(db) say rc oosqlErrMsg(db) call oosqlFinalize stmt say oosqlClose(db) /* Output: 5 unable to close due to unfinalized statements or unfinished backups 0 */

section.title: oosqlColumnBlob
section.para: Returns the value of a column of the current result row of a prepared statement as a BLOB.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
stmt [required]
The handle to a statement prepared by oosqlPrepare. The handle must not be null, and the statement must not have been finalized: see the rules for statement handles.
column [required]
The number of the column in the result row, 1 for the first column.

A string with the bytes of the value, including any NUL characters. A value that is not a BLOB is converted: text is returned as is, and a number as its text representation. An empty BLOB, a NULL value, and a column that is out of range return the empty string.

What is said here applies to all the routines that return the value of a column, such as oosqlColumnBlob, oosqlColumnInt, or oosqlColumnText: they return a value of the current result row, so they are meaningful only after oosqlStep has returned ROW, and until the statement is stepped again, reset, or finalized. If they are invoked at any other time, the result is undefined. SQLite converts the value to the type asked for when the column holds a value of another type.
A NULL value is the empty string. Use oosqlColumnType to tell a NULL value from an empty one.
The functionality of the oosqlColumnBlob routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_column_blob API.
The columnBlob method of the ooSQLiteStmt class does the same for a statement object.

This example reads the picture of a row, and displays its size and its bytes in hexadecimal:
rc = oosqlExec(db, "UPDATE foods SET picture = x'89504E470D0A1A0A' WHERE id = 1;") rc = oosqlPrepare(db, "SELECT picture FROM foods WHERE id = 1;", 'stmt') if oosqlStep(stmt) == .ooSQLite~ROW then do picture = oosqlColumnBlob(stmt, 1) say oosqlColumnBytes(stmt, 1) picture~length picture~c2x end call oosqlFinalize stmt /* Output: 8 8 89504E470D0A1A0A */

section.title: oosqlColumnBytes
section.para: Returns the size in bytes of the value of a column of the current result row of a prepared statement.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
stmt [required]
The handle to a statement prepared by oosqlPrepare. The handle must not be null, and the statement must not have been finalized: see the rules for statement handles.
column [required]
The number of the column in the result row, 1 for the first column.
The size of a BLOB, or of the UTF-8 text of any other value: the number 3.9 has 3 bytes. A NULL value, and a column that is out of range, have 0 bytes.
See the remarks of oosqlColumnBlob for when the values of a row can be retrieved.
The functionality of the oosqlColumnBytes routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_column_bytes API.
The columnBytes method of the ooSQLiteStmt class does the same for a statement object.
See the example of oosqlColumnBlob.

section.title: oosqlColumnCount
section.para: Returns the number of columns in the result set of a prepared statement.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
stmt [required]
The handle to a statement prepared by oosqlPrepare. The handle must not be null, and the statement must not have been finalized: see the rules for statement handles.
The number of columns, or 0 for a statement that returns no data, such as an INSERT or an UPDATE.
The number of columns is known as soon as the statement is prepared: this routine can be invoked before oosqlStep. Compare with oosqlDataCount.
The functionality of the oosqlColumnCount routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_column_count API.
The columnCount method of the ooSQLiteStmt class does the same for a statement object.
See the example of oosqlColumnName.

section.title: oosqlColumnDatabaseName
section.para: Returns the name of the database that a result column of a prepared statement comes from.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
stmt [required]
The handle to a statement prepared by oosqlPrepare. The handle must not be null, and the statement must not have been finalized: see the rules for statement handles.
column [required]
The number of the column in the result row, 1 for the first column.

The name of the database: main for the main database, temp for the temporary database, or the name given to an attached database. When the result column is an expression, not a column of a table, and when the column is out of range, the string NULL is returned.
The name is known as soon as the statement is prepared: this routine can be invoked before oosqlStep. oosqlColumnTableName and oosqlColumnOriginName give the table and the column of the table.
The functionality of the oosqlColumnDatabaseName routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_column_database_name API.
The columnDataBaseName method of the ooSQLiteStmt class does the same for a statement object.
See the example of oosqlColumnName.

section.title: oosqlColumnDeclType
section.para: Returns the declared type of the table column that a result column of a prepared statement comes from.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
stmt [required]
The handle to a statement prepared by oosqlPrepare. The handle must not be null, and the statement must not have been finalized: see the rules for statement handles.
column [required]
The number of the column in the result row, 1 for the first column.

The type as written in the CREATE TABLE statement, such as INTEGER or TEXT. When the result column is an expression, not a column of a table, when the column of the table was declared without a type, and when the column is out of range, the empty string is returned.
SQLite is dynamically typed: the declared type does not say what type a value has. Use oosqlColumnType for the type of a value in the current row.
The functionality of the oosqlColumnDeclType routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_column_decltype API.
The columnDeclType method of the ooSQLiteStmt class does the same for a statement object.
See the example of oosqlColumnName.

section.title: &changed11;oosqlColumnDouble
section.para: Returns the value of a column of the current result row of a prepared statement as a floating point number.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
stmt [required]
The handle to a statement prepared by oosqlPrepare. The handle must not be null, and the statement must not have been finalized: see the rules for statement handles.
column [required]
The number of the column in the result row, 1 for the first column.

The value as a number, with all its precision: the shortest number, of up to 17 significant digits, that is converted back to the same floating point value. Text that starts with a number is converted to that number; a NULL value, and a column that is out of range, return 0.

&changed11;Before ooSQLite 1.1, the number was returned with 9 significant digits only: 3.141592653589793 was returned as 3.14159265. A Rexx program computes with 9 digits unless it sets NUMERIC DIGITS: the number keeps its precision, but an arithmetic operation on it is rounded to the current setting.
See the remarks of oosqlColumnBlob for when the values of a row can be retrieved.
The functionality of the oosqlColumnDouble routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_column_double API.
The columnDouble method of the ooSQLiteStmt class does the same for a statement object.
See the example of oosqlColumnType.

section.title: oosqlColumnIndex
section.para: Returns the number of the result column of a prepared statement with the given name.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
stmt [required]
The handle to a statement prepared by oosqlPrepare. The handle must not be null, and the statement must not have been finalized: see the rules for statement handles.
columnName [required]
The name of the result column, as returned by oosqlColumnName: for a column with an AS clause, it is the name given there. The comparison is case insensitive.
The number of the column, 1 for the first column, or 0 if the result set has no column with that name. When several columns have the same name, the number of the first one is returned.
The column names are known as soon as the statement is prepared: this routine can be invoked before oosqlStep.
This routine is an ooSQLite enhancement, there is no similar SQLite API.
The columnIndex method of the ooSQLiteStmt class does the same for a statement object.

This example finds the columns it needs by name, so that it does not depend on their order in the query:
rc = oosqlPrepare(db, "SELECT id, name, price FROM foods ORDER BY price DESC;", 'stmt') nameCol = oosqlColumnIndex(stmt, 'name') priceCol = oosqlColumnIndex(stmt, 'PRICE') do while oosqlStep(stmt) == .ooSQLite~ROW say oosqlColumnText(stmt, nameCol)~left(20) oosqlColumnText(stmt, priceCol, '') end call oosqlFinalize stmt /* Output: Bacon 3.75 Bagels, raisin 1.5 Bagels 1.25 Cheese */

section.title: oosqlColumnInt
section.para: Returns the value of a column of the current result row of a prepared statement as a 32-bit integer.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
stmt [required]
The handle to a statement prepared by oosqlPrepare. The handle must not be null, and the statement must not have been finalized: see the rules for statement handles.
column [required]
The number of the column in the result row, 1 for the first column.

The value as a whole number. A floating point value is truncated, so 3.9 is 3, and text that starts with a number is converted to that number. A NULL value, and a column that is out of range, return 0.

When the value does not fit in 32 bits, only its lower 32 bits are returned, and the result is not meaningful: use oosqlColumnInt64 for values that can be that large. See the remarks of oosqlColumnBlob for when the values of a row can be retrieved.
The functionality of the oosqlColumnInt routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_column_int API.
The columnInt method of the ooSQLiteStmt class does the same for a statement object.
See the examples of oosqlPrepare and oosqlReset.

section.title: oosqlColumnInt64
section.para: Returns the value of a column of the current result row of a prepared statement as a 64-bit integer.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
stmt [required]
The handle to a statement prepared by oosqlPrepare. The handle must not be null, and the statement must not have been finalized: see the rules for statement handles.
column [required]
The number of the column in the result row, 1 for the first column.
The value as a whole number, converted as oosqlColumnInt does. A NULL value, and a column that is out of range, return 0.
See the remarks of oosqlColumnBlob for when the values of a row can be retrieved.
The functionality of the oosqlColumnInt64 routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_column_int64 API.
The columnInt64 method of the ooSQLiteStmt class does the same for a statement object.

section.title: oosqlColumnName
section.para: Returns the name of a result column of a prepared statement.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
stmt [required]
The handle to a statement prepared by oosqlPrepare. The handle must not be null, and the statement must not have been finalized: see the rules for statement handles.
column [required]
The number of the column in the result row, 1 for the first column.

The name of the column: for a column with an AS clause, the name given there; otherwise, the name SQLite gives it, which for a column of a table is normally the name of the table column, and for an expression is normally the text of the expression. For a column that is out of range, the string NULL is returned.

The names are known as soon as the statement is prepared: this routine can be invoked before oosqlStep. SQLite does not guarantee the name of a column without an AS clause, so a program that depends on the names should give them.
The functionality of the oosqlColumnName routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_column_name API.
The columnName method of the ooSQLiteStmt class does the same for a statement object.

This example displays, for each column of a query, its name, the column, table and database it comes from, and its declared type. The last column is an expression, so it comes from no table:
rc = oosqlPrepare(db, "SELECT id, name AS food, price, price * 2 FROM foods;", 'stmt') do i = 1 to oosqlColumnCount(stmt) say i oosqlColumnName(stmt, i)~left(10) oosqlColumnOriginName(stmt, i)~left(8) - oosqlColumnTableName(stmt, i)~left(8) oosqlColumnDatabaseName(stmt, i)~left(6) - oosqlColumnDeclType(stmt, i) end call oosqlFinalize stmt /* Output: 1 id id foods main INTEGER 2 food name foods main TEXT 3 price price foods main REAL 4 price * 2 NULL NULL NULL */

section.title: oosqlColumnOriginName
section.para: Returns the name of the table column that a result column of a prepared statement comes from.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
stmt [required]
The handle to a statement prepared by oosqlPrepare. The handle must not be null, and the statement must not have been finalized: see the rules for statement handles.
column [required]
The number of the column in the result row, 1 for the first column.

The name of the column in its table, without the alias that an AS clause may give it. When the result column is an expression, not a column of a table, and when the column is out of range, the string NULL is returned.
The name is known as soon as the statement is prepared: this routine can be invoked before oosqlStep.
The functionality of the oosqlColumnOriginName routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_column_origin_name API.
The columnOriginName method of the ooSQLiteStmt class does the same for a statement object.
See the example of oosqlColumnName.

section.title: oosqlColumnTableName
section.para: Returns the name of the table that a result column of a prepared statement comes from.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
stmt [required]
The handle to a statement prepared by oosqlPrepare. The handle must not be null, and the statement must not have been finalized: see the rules for statement handles.
column [required]
The number of the column in the result row, 1 for the first column.

The name of the table, without the alias that the query may give it. When the result column is an expression, not a column of a table, and when the column is out of range, the string NULL is returned.
The name is known as soon as the statement is prepared: this routine can be invoked before oosqlStep.
The functionality of the oosqlColumnTableName routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_column_table_name API.
The columnTableName method of the ooSQLiteStmt class does the same for a statement object.
See the example of oosqlColumnName.

section.title: oosqlColumnText
section.para: Returns the value of a column of the current result row of a prepared statement as a string.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
stmt [required]
The handle to a statement prepared by oosqlPrepare. The handle must not be null, and the statement must not have been finalized: see the rules for statement handles.
column [required]
The number of the column in the result row, 1 for the first column.
nullObj [optional]
The object to return for a NULL value. The default is the .nil object.

The value as a string: text as is, a number as its text representation, and a BLOB with all its bytes, as oosqlColumnBlob returns it. For a NULL value, and for a column that is out of range, nullObj is returned.
This is the routine used most to retrieve values, because any value can be represented as a string. See the remarks of oosqlColumnBlob for when the values of a row can be retrieved.

The functionality of the oosqlColumnText routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_column_text API. For a BLOB, SQLite would return only the bytes before the first NUL character; ooSQLite returns all of them.
The columnText method of the ooSQLiteStmt class does the same for a statement object; it has no nullObj argument, but takes the value to return for NULL from the attribute of the statement.

This example displays the price of each food, or unknown if it has no price:
rc = oosqlPrepare(db, "SELECT name, price FROM foods ORDER BY id;", 'stmt') do while oosqlStep(stmt) == .ooSQLite~ROW say oosqlColumnText(stmt, 1)~left(16) oosqlColumnText(stmt, 2, 'unknown') end call oosqlFinalize stmt /* Output: Bagels 1.25 Bagels, raisin 1.5 Bacon 3.75 Cheese unknown */

section.title: oosqlColumnType
section.para: Returns the datatype of the value of a column of the current result row of a prepared statement.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
stmt [required]
The handle to a statement prepared by oosqlPrepare. The handle must not be null, and the statement must not have been finalized: see the rules for statement handles.
column [required]
The number of the column in the result row, 1 for the first column.
One of the Fundamental Datatype constants: INTEGER, FLOAT, TEXT, BLOB, or SQLNULL. A column that is out of range is SQLNULL.

SQLite is dynamically typed: the same column can hold values of different types in different rows, whatever its declared type. Retrieving a value with a routine of another type, such as oosqlColumnText for an integer, can convert the value in place, and then the type returned by this routine afterwards is undefined: invoke oosqlColumnType before retrieving the value. See the remarks of oosqlColumnBlob for when the values of a row can be retrieved.
The functionality of the oosqlColumnType routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_column_type API.
The columnType method of the ooSQLiteStmt class does the same for a statement object.

This example formats the price of each food according to its type:
rc = oosqlPrepare(db, "SELECT name, price FROM foods;", 'stmt') do while oosqlStep(stmt) == .ooSQLite~ROW select when oosqlColumnType(stmt, 2) == .ooSQLite~SQLNULL then price = 'n/a' when oosqlColumnType(stmt, 2) == .ooSQLite~FLOAT then price = oosqlColumnDouble(stmt, 2)~format(, 2) otherwise price = '?' end say oosqlColumnText(stmt, 1)~left(20) price end call oosqlFinalize stmt /* Output: Bagels 1.25 Bagels, raisin 1.50 Bacon 3.75 Cheese n/a */

section.title: oosqlColumnValue
section.para: Returns the value of a column of the current result row of a prepared statement, in the form needed to bind it to a host parameter with oosqlBindValue.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
stmt [required]
The handle to a statement prepared by oosqlPrepare. The handle must not be null, and the statement must not have been finalized: see the rules for statement handles.
column [required]
The number of the column in the result row, 1 for the first column.
A Pointer object, which points to an SQLite sqlite3_value structure.

The only use of the value returned is to pass it to oosqlBindValue, which binds it to a parameter of a statement keeping its datatype. It is only valid while the statement stays on the same result row: see the remarks of oosqlBindValue.
The functionality of the oosqlColumnValue routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_column_value API. The value is what SQLite calls an unprotected sqlite3_value.
The columnValue method of the ooSQLiteStmt class does the same for a statement object.
See the example of oosqlBindValue.

section.title: oosqlCollationNeeded
section.para: Registers a routine that is called when a statement needs a collation sequence that is not defined.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
db [required]
The handle to a database connection, as set by oosqlOpen. The handle must not be null.
rtnName [required]
The name of the public routine to call for each undefined collation, or the empty string to remove the routine registered before. See the rules for callback routines.
userData [optional]
Any object, passed to the routine as its third argument. If it is omitted, the routine receives .nil.
Returns OK on success, or one of the Result Code constants on error.

The routine is called with three arguments: the handle to the database connection, the name of the collation, as it is written in the SQL, and the user data. To make the collation available, the routine defines it with oosqlCreateCollation on that handle. It must return a whole number, which is ignored. If it does not define the collation, the statement fails with no such collation sequence.
The functionality of the oosqlCollationNeeded routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_collation_needed API.
The collationNeeded method of the ooSQLiteConnection class does the same with a method of an object; see also collationNeededCallBack.

This example defines the collation REVERSE only when a query uses it:
rc = oosqlCollationNeeded(db, 'defineCollation') rows. = oosqlExec(db, "SELECT name FROM foods ORDER BY name COLLATE REVERSE;", .true) do i = 1 to rows.0 say rows.i['NAME'] end /* Output: Collation needed: REVERSE Cheese Bagels, raisin Bagels Bacon */
::routine defineCollation public use arg db, name say 'Collation needed:' name if name~upper == 'REVERSE' then call oosqlCreateCollation db, 'compareReverse', name return 0
::routine compareReverse public use arg a, b if a < b then return 1 if a > b then return -1 return 0

section.title: oosqlCommitHook
section.para: Registers a routine that is called whenever a transaction is about to be committed.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
db [required]
The handle to a database connection, as set by oosqlOpen. The handle must not be null.
rtnName [required]
The name of the public routine to call before each commit, or the empty string to remove the routine registered before. See the rules for callback routines.
userData [optional]
Any object, passed to the routine as its only argument. If it is omitted, the routine receives .nil.
Returns the userData of the routine that was registered before, or .nil if there was none, or it had no user data.

The routine is called with one argument, the user data. It must return a whole number: 0 lets the commit go on; any other value turns the COMMIT into a ROLLBACK, and the statement fails with CONSTRAINT_COMMITHOOK (531). In autocommit mode, every statement that changes the database is committed when it ends, so the routine is called for each one.
The routine must not use the connection: it must not prepare or execute SQL on it.
The functionality of the oosqlCommitHook routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_commit_hook API.
The commitHook method of the ooSQLiteConnection class does the same with a method of an object; see also commitHookCallBack.

This example counts the commits made by two calls to oosqlExec, using a Directory object as the user data:
counter = .directory~new counter~commits = 0 rc = oosqlCommitHook(db, 'countCommits', counter) rc = oosqlExec(db, "UPDATE foods SET price = price + 1 WHERE type_id = 1;") rc = oosqlExec(db, "BEGIN; DELETE FROM foods WHERE id = 4; INSERT INTO foods(name) VALUES('Toast'); COMMIT;") say counter~commits 'commit(s)' rc = oosqlCommitHook(db, '') /* Output: 2 commit(s) */
::routine countCommits public use arg counter counter~commits += 1 return 0
