section.title: oosqlCompileOptionUsed
section.para: Tests if an option was used at compile time when the SQLite library that ooSQLite uses was built.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
name [required]
The name of the option, such as ENABLE_FTS5. The SQLITE_ prefix can be omitted, and the comparison is case insensitive. An option with a value can be given with it, as in THREADSAFE=1, to test the value too.
Returns true if the option was used, and false if it was not.

The options tell which optional features are in the library: full text search (ENABLE_FTS5), R*Tree indexes (ENABLE_RTREE), the math functions (ENABLE_MATH_FUNCTIONS), and others. oosqlCompileOptionGet lists them all.
The functionality of the oosqlCompileOptionUsed routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_compileoption_used API.
The compileOptionUsed method of the ooSQLite class does the same.

This example tests some options:
do option over .array~of('ENABLE_FTS5', 'ENABLE_RTREE', 'ENABLE_ICU', 'THREADSAFE=1') say left(option, 14) oosqlCompileOptionUsed(option) end /* Output: ENABLE_FTS5 1 ENABLE_RTREE 1 ENABLE_ICU 0 THREADSAFE=1 1 */

section.title: oosqlComplete
section.para: Tests if a text seems to form one or more complete SQL statements.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
sql [required]
The text to test.
Returns true if the text ends with a complete statement, and false if more text is needed.

A statement is complete when it ends with a semicolon that is not inside a string, a quoted name, or a comment, and it is not the first part of a CREATE TRIGGER statement, which needs its END;. The statement is not parsed, so it can be complete and still have errors. The routine is useful for programs that read SQL a line at a time, to know when to execute what they have read. Text with only white space and comments is not complete; a lone semicolon is.
The functionality of the oosqlComplete routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_complete API.
The complete method of the ooSQLite class does the same.

This example joins lines until they form a complete statement. The semicolon inside the string of the second statement does not end it:
lines = .array~of("SELECT name", " FROM foods", " WHERE price > 2;", "SELECT ';' AS semicolon;") sql = '' do line over lines sql = sql line if oosqlComplete(sql) then do say 'Complete:' sql~space sql = '' end end /* Output: Complete: SELECT name FROM foods WHERE price > 2; Complete: SELECT ';' AS semicolon; */

section.title: oosqlCreateCollation
section.para: Defines a collation sequence, with a routine that compares two strings.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
db [required]
The handle to a database connection, as set by oosqlOpen. The handle must not be null.
rtnName [required]
The name of the public routine to call to compare two strings, or the empty string to remove the routine registered before. See the rules for callback routines.
collationName [required]
The name of the collation, used in SQL in the COLLATE clause. Case is not significant.
userData [optional]
Any object, passed to the routine as its third argument. If it is omitted, the routine receives .nil.
Returns OK on success, or one of the Result Code constants on error.

The routine is called with three arguments: the two strings to compare, and the user data. It must return a negative number if the first string sorts before the second, 0 if they are equal, and a positive number if it sorts after. It must always give the same result for the same strings.
To remove the collation, pass the empty string as rtnName with its collationName. A collation can also be defined only when a statement needs it, with oosqlCollationNeeded.
The functionality of the oosqlCreateCollation routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_create_collation_v2 API.
The createCollation method of the ooSQLiteConnection class does the same with a method of an object.

This example sorts the names of the foods without regard to case:
rc = oosqlExec(db, "INSERT INTO foods(name) VALUES('bacon bits');") rc = oosqlCreateCollation(db, 'compareNoCase', 'NOCASEREXX') rows. = oosqlExec(db, "SELECT name FROM foods ORDER BY name COLLATE NOCASEREXX;", .true) do i = 1 to rows.0 say rows.i['NAME'] end /* Output: Bacon bacon bits Bagels Bagels, raisin Cheese */
::routine compareNoCase public use arg a, b a = a~upper b = b~upper if a < b then return -1 if a > b then return 1 return 0

section.title: &changed11;oosqlCreateFunction
section.para: Define a SQL function implemented in Rexx:
Define a SQL aggregate implemented in Rexx:
Remove a SQL function or aggregate implemented in Rexx:

Adds or removes a user defined SQL function or aggregate on a database connection. This is the classic interface equivalent of the createFunction method of the ooSQLiteConnection class, which explains functions and aggregates in more detail. Here the callbacks are routines instead of methods.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
db [required]
The handle to the database connection.
name [required]
The name of the function, the name that is used for it in SQL statements.
countArgs [required when defining, optional when removing]
The number of arguments the function takes, or -1 if it takes any number of arguments. SQLite identifies a function by its name and its number of arguments.
&changed11;When removing a function, this is the number of arguments of the function to remove. If it is omitted, all the functions with this name are removed, whatever their number of arguments.
funcRtn [required for a function]
The name of the routine that implements the function. When it is given, stepRtn and finalRtn must be omitted.
stepRtn [required for an aggregate]
The name of the routine that is invoked for each row of the aggregate.
finalRtn [required for an aggregate]
The name of the routine that is invoked once all the rows have been processed, to produce the result of the aggregate.
userData [optional]
Any Rexx object. It is sent to every invocation of the callback routines. If it is omitted, the routines get the .nil object instead.
Returns a SQLite result code.

The routines must be public routines (::routine name public) of the package that invokes oosqlCreateFunction. They get the same arguments as the callback methods of createFunction, except that the first one is the database connection handle. The values are read with the oosqlValue routines, like oosqlValueInt, and the result is set with the oosqlResult routines, like oosqlResultInt.
&changed11;When an aggregate runs over no rows, the step routine is never invoked, and the final routine gets .nil as the aggregate object.

&changed11;To remove a function, omit the routine names. Functions with the same name and a different number of arguments are different functions, and can be defined side by side. When countArgs is given, only the function with that number of arguments is removed; when it is omitted, all the functions with this name defined in Rexx are removed. Removing a function that does not exist is not an error.
The functionality of the oosqlCreateFunction routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_create_function_v2 API.

This example defines a double function and a my_sum aggregate, uses them, and then removes the function:
call oosqlOpen ":memory:", "db"
call oosqlCreateFunction db, "double", 1, "doubleRtn" call oosqlCreateFunction db, "my_sum", 1, , "sumStep", "sumFinal"
rows = oosqlExec(db, "SELECT double(21) AS d, my_sum(x) AS s FROM t;", .true)
call oosqlCreateFunction db, "double"
::routine doubleRtn public use arg db, context, userData, value call oosqlResultInt context, oosqlValueInt(value) * 2 return 0
::routine sumStep public use arg db, context, sum, userData, value if sum == .nil then sum = .Directory~new~~put(0, "TOTAL") sum["TOTAL"] += oosqlValueInt(value) return sum
::routine sumFinal public use arg db, context, sum, userData if sum == .nil then call oosqlResultNull context else call oosqlResultInt context, sum["TOTAL"] return 0

section.title: oosqlDataCount
section.para: Returns the number of columns in the current result row of a prepared statement.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
stmt [required]
The handle to a statement prepared by oosqlPrepare. The handle must not be null, and the statement must not have been finalized: see the rules for statement handles.

The number of columns of the current row: the same as oosqlColumnCount after oosqlStep has returned ROW, and 0 when there is no current row: before the statement is stepped, after oosqlStep has returned DONE or an error, and after a reset.
The functionality of the oosqlDataCount routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_data_count API.
The dataCount method of the ooSQLiteStmt class does the same for a statement object.

This example shows the difference between oosqlDataCount and oosqlColumnCount:
rc = oosqlPrepare(db, "SELECT id, name FROM foods;", 'stmt') say oosqlColumnCount(stmt) oosqlDataCount(stmt) -- 2 0 rc = oosqlStep(stmt) say oosqlColumnCount(stmt) oosqlDataCount(stmt) -- 2 2 call oosqlFinalize stmt

section.title: oosqlDbFileName
section.para: Returns the file name of a database of a database connection.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
db [required]
The handle to a database connection, as set by oosqlOpen. The handle must not be null, and the connection must not have been closed: see oosqlClose.
name [required]
The name of the database: main for the main database, temp, or the name of an attached database.
The full path of the file of the database. For a database that does not exist on the connection, and for a temporary or in-memory database, the empty string is returned.
The path is absolute, even when the database was opened with a relative path or a URI.
The functionality of the oosqlDbFileName routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_db_filename API.
The dbFileName method of the ooSQLiteConnection class does the same for a connection object.

This example attaches an in-memory database, and displays, for some database names, the values of oosqlDbReadOnly and oosqlDbFileName:
rc = oosqlExec(db, "ATTACH DATABASE ':memory:' AS scratch;") do name over .array~of('main', 'scratch', 'temp', 'other') say name~left(8) oosqlDbReadOnly(db, name)~right(2) '['oosqlDbFileName(db, name)']' end /* Output might be: main 0 [/home/rexx/ooFoods.rdbx] scratch 0 [] temp -1 [] other -1 [] */

section.title: oosqlDbHandle
section.para: Returns the database connection of a prepared statement.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
stmt [required]
The handle to a statement prepared by oosqlPrepare. The handle must not be null, and the statement must not have been finalized: see the rules for statement handles.

The handle to the database connection that was used to prepare the statement. It is the same handle that was passed to oosqlPrepare, and it can be used in any routine that needs a database connection.
The functionality of the oosqlDbHandle routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_db_handle API.
The dbHandle method of the ooSQLiteStmt class returns the connection object of a statement object.

This example uses the connection of the statement to find how many rows it deleted:
rc = oosqlPrepare(db, "DELETE FROM foods WHERE price IS NULL;", 'stmt') rc = oosqlStep(stmt) say oosqlChanges(oosqlDbHandle(stmt)) 'row(s) deleted' call oosqlFinalize stmt /* Output: 1 row(s) deleted */

section.title: oosqlDbMutex
section.para: Returns the mutex that serializes the access to a database connection.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
db [required]
The handle to a database connection, as set by oosqlOpen. The handle must not be null, and the connection must not have been closed: see oosqlClose.
A handle to the mutex, which can be used with oosqlMutexEnter, oosqlMutexTry, and oosqlMutexLeave. If the connection is not in the serialized threading mode, which is unlikely, the handle is null.

The mutex belongs to SQLite, which uses it to protect the connection: never free it with oosqlMutexFree. Holding the mutex keeps other threads from using the connection, so it must be left as soon as possible, once for each time it was entered.
The functionality of the oosqlDbMutex routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_db_mutex API.
The dbMutex method of the ooSQLiteConnection class returns an ooSQLiteMutex object.

This example holds the mutex of a connection while it uses the connection:
mtx = oosqlDbMutex(db) call oosqlMutexEnter mtx -- No other thread can use the connection here say oosqlChanges(db) call oosqlMutexLeave mtx

section.title: oosqlDbReadOnly
section.para: Tests if a database of a database connection is read only.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
db [required]
The handle to a database connection, as set by oosqlOpen. The handle must not be null, and the connection must not have been closed: see oosqlClose.
name [required]
The name of the database: main for the main database, temp, or the name of an attached database.
Returns 1 if the database is read only, 0 if it can be written, and -1 if the connection has no database with that name.
The temporary database, temp, only exists once something has been created in it: until then, -1 is returned for it.
The functionality of the oosqlDbReadOnly routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_db_readonly API.
The dbReadOnly method of the ooSQLiteConnection class does the same for a connection object.
See the example of oosqlDbFileName.

section.title: oosqlDbReleaseMemory
section.para: Makes SQLite free as much heap memory as it can from a database connection.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
db [required]
The handle to a database connection, as set by oosqlOpen. The handle must not be null, and the connection must not have been closed: see oosqlClose.
Returns OK.
The memory freed is mostly the page cache of the connection that is not in use. oosqlReleaseMemory frees memory from all the connections of the process.
The functionality of the oosqlDbReleaseMemory routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_db_release_memory API.
The dbReleaseMemory method of the ooSQLiteConnection class does the same for a connection object.

section.title: oosqlDbStatus
section.para: Retrieves runtime status information about a database connection, and optionally resets its highwater mark.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
db [required]
The handle to an open database connection, as set by oosqlOpen. The handle must not be null.
op [required]
The status parameter to retrieve, one of the DB Status Parameter constants, such as DBSTATUS_CACHE_USED.
result [required]
A Stem object, not the name of a stem, in which the values are returned. Raises a syntax error, 88.900, if it is not a Stem object. On success, these tails of the stem are set: CURRENT, the current value of the parameter, and HIGHWATER, its highest recorded value.
reset [optional]
If true, the highwater mark is reset to the current value after it is retrieved. The default is false.
Returns OK on success, or ERROR if op is not a valid DB status parameter. On error, the stem is not changed; oosqlErrMsg does not describe this error.

Many parameters, such as DBSTATUS_CACHE_USED, record only the current value, and their highwater mark is always 0. The status parameters of SQLite grow with new versions of SQLite; the DB Status Parameter constants are those of the SQLite embedded in ooSQLite.
The functionality of the oosqlDbStatus routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_db_status API.
The dbStatus method of the ooSQLiteConnection class does the same, with a Directory object instead of a stem.

This example displays how much memory the page cache and the schema of a connection use, after a query:
rc = oosqlExec(db, "SELECT count(*) FROM foods;") rc = oosqlDbStatus(db, .ooSQLite~DBSTATUS_CACHE_USED, s.) if rc == .ooSQLite~OK then say 'Page cache:' s.current 'bytes' rc = oosqlDbStatus(db, .ooSQLite~DBSTATUS_SCHEMA_USED, s.) if rc == .ooSQLite~OK then say 'Schema: ' s.current 'bytes' /* Output might be: Page cache: 13616 bytes Schema: 2136 bytes */

section.title: oosqlEnableLoadExtension
section.para: Allows or forbids loading SQLite extension libraries on a database connection.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
db [required]
The handle to a database connection, as set by oosqlOpen. The handle must not be null, and the connection must not have been closed: see oosqlClose.
on [optional]
True to allow loading extensions with oosqlLoadExtension, false to forbid it. The default is false.
Returns OK.

Loading extensions is forbidden by default, because an extension library can run any code. It is good practice to allow it only while the extensions are loaded. The SQL function load_extension() is also allowed or forbidden by this routine.
The functionality of the oosqlEnableLoadExtension routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_enable_load_extension API.
See the example of oosqlLoadExtension.

section.title: oosqlErrCode
section.para: Returns the result code of the last error on a database connection.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
db [required]
The handle to a database connection, as set by oosqlOpen. The handle must not be null, and the connection must not have been closed: see oosqlClose.
One of the Result Code constants, often an extended one, or OK if there has been no error.

The error code and message describe the last SQLite call on the connection that failed, if the calls after it did not set them again: a call that succeeds can reset them, or leave them as they were, so they are only meaningful right after a routine has returned an error. Some errors are not recorded in the connection: those detected by ooSQLite itself, the errors of oosqlLoadExtension, and those of oosqlDbStatus.

ooSQLite enables extended result codes for every connection, so the code is often an extended one, such as CONSTRAINT_PRIMARYKEY (1555), rather than CONSTRAINT (19). oosqlErrCode and oosqlExtendedErrCode are the same routine.
oosqlErrMsg describes the error, and oosqlErrStr gives the general description of a result code.
The functionality of the oosqlErrCode routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_extended_errcode API.
The errCode method of the ooSQLiteConnection class does the same for a connection object.

This example executes an INSERT that fails, because the table already has a row with that id, and displays the error:
rc = oosqlExec(db, "INSERT INTO foods(id, name) VALUES(1, 'Toast');") say rc say oosqlErrCode(db) oosqlErrMsg(db) say oosqlErrStr(oosqlErrCode(db)) /* Output: SQLite Error: rc = 1555, UNIQUE constraint failed: foods.id 1555 UNIQUE constraint failed: foods.id constraint failed */

section.title: oosqlErrMsg
section.para: Returns the English-language description of the last error on a database connection.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
db [required]
The handle to a database connection, as set by oosqlOpen. The handle must not be null, and the connection must not have been closed: see oosqlClose.
The description, such as no such table: food. If there has been no error, not an error is returned.

See the remarks of oosqlErrCode, which returns the code of the same error. The message describes the specific error, and can name the table or the column involved; oosqlErrStr only gives the general description of a result code.
The functionality of the oosqlErrMsg routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_errmsg API.
The errMsg method of the ooSQLiteConnection class does the same for a connection object.
See the example of oosqlErrCode.

section.title: oosqlErrStr
section.para: Retrieves the English language descriptive string for a result code.

listitem.para: The arguments are:
One of the result code constants, or one of the ooSQLite specific result code, whose descriptive sting is to be retrieved.
Returns the descriptive, English language, string for the specified result code.

This routine is useful for getting the description of a result code without needing a open database connection. The oosqlErrMsg routine will return the descriptive string for the most recent result code associated with the database connection, but the routine requires a handle to an open database connection. The oosqlErrStr routine can be used at any time to get the descriptive string for a result code.
The functionality of the oosqlErrStr function is similar to that of the sqlite3_errstr SQLite API

This example is a small snippet of code to print out the description of the first 27 result codes. Inspection of the ooSQLite.cls file shows us that the first 27 result code constants are in numerically consecutive order:
first = .ooSQLite~OK last = .ooSQLite~NOTADB
do i = first to last say oosqlErrStr(i) end say
/* Output would be:
not an error SQL logic error or missing database unknown error access permission denied callback requested query abort database is locked database table is locked out of memory attempt to write a readonly database interrupted disk I/O error database disk image is malformed unknown operation database or disk is full unable to open database file locking protocol table contains no data database schema has changed string or blob too big constraint failed datatype mismatch library routine called out of sequence large file support is disabled authorization denied auxiliary database format error bind or column index out of range file is encrypted or is not a database
*/

section.title: oosqlExec
section.para: Executes one or more SQL statements, and optionally returns their result rows, or calls a routine for each row.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
db [required]
The handle to a database connection, as set by oosqlOpen. The handle must not be null, and the connection must not have been closed: see oosqlClose.
sql [required]
The SQL to execute: one statement, or several, separated by semicolons. They are executed in order, until one of them fails.
doCallback [optional]
False, the default, to just execute the SQL: the return is a result code. True to get the result rows: as a result set returned by oosqlExec, or, when rtnName is given, by calling that routine once for each row.
format [optional]
The format of the result set, and of each row, one of the Result Set Format constants. It is ignored when doCallback is false. The default is OO_STEM_OF_STEMS. The formats are:
OO_STEM_OF_STEMS
A stem whose tail 0 is the number of rows, and whose tail i is row i, itself a stem whose tails are the names of the columns, in upper case: rows.i['NAME'].
OO_CLASSIC_STEM
A single stem with compound tails: rows.i.NAME, and rows.0 for the number of rows.
OO_ARRAY_OF_DIRECTORIES
An array with a Directory object for each row, whose indexes are the names of the columns.
OO_ARRAY_OF_ARRAYS
An array whose first item is an array with the names of the columns, and each following item an array with the values of a row.
rtnName [optional]
The name of a routine to call for each result row, instead of building a result set. It must be a public routine of the program that calls oosqlExec: see the rules for callback routines. It is ignored when doCallback is false. The routine is called with two arguments: the row, in the format given by format, and the number of the row, 1 for the first one. It must return a whole number: 0 to go on, or any other value to stop executing the SQL.
When the SQL executes without error, OK if doCallback is false or rtnName is given, and otherwise the result set, which is empty if the SQL returns no rows.

When there is an error, a string with the result code and the description of the error, such as SQLite Error: rc = 1, no such table: food. The code is also returned by oosqlErrCode. When the callback routine stops the execution, the error is ABORT (4), query aborted.

A NULL value is not set in the row: with the stem formats, the tail of that column is not assigned, and has its default value, its own name, which can be tested with hasIndex; with the other formats, the item is .nil.
For SQL that returns rows, and needs values from the program, it is better to prepare a statement with oosqlPrepare, bind the values, and step it: the values do not need to be quoted.
Raises a syntax error if format is not one of the format constants, or if there is no public routine named rtnName.
The functionality of the oosqlExec routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_exec API.

The exec method of the ooSQLiteConnection class does the same for a connection object, with the result rows in the format of its recordFormat attribute, and with a method of an object as the callback.

This example executes an UPDATE, displays the rows of a query from the result set, and then the rows of another query from a callback routine:
rc = oosqlExec(db, "UPDATE foods SET price = 1.75 WHERE name = 'Cheese';") if rc <> .ooSQLite~OK then say rc
rows. = oosqlExec(db, "SELECT id, name FROM foods WHERE type_id = 1;", .true) do i = 1 to rows.0 say rows.i['ID'] rows.i['NAME'] end
rc = oosqlExec(db, "SELECT name, price FROM foods;", .true, , 'showFood') /* Output: 1 Bagels 2 Bagels, raisin 1 Bagels 1.25 2 Bagels, raisin 1.5 3 Bacon 3.75 4 Cheese 1.75 */
::routine showFood public use arg row, rowNumber say rowNumber row['NAME'] row['PRICE'] return 0

section.title: oosqlExtendedErrCode
section.para: Returns the extended result code of the last error on a database connection.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
db [required]
The handle to a database connection, as set by oosqlOpen. The handle must not be null, and the connection must not have been closed: see oosqlClose.
One of the Result Code constants, or OK if there has been no error.
This routine is the same as oosqlErrCode: ooSQLite enables extended result codes for every connection, so both return them. It is provided for completeness. See the remarks of oosqlErrCode.
The functionality of the oosqlExtendedErrCode routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_extended_errcode API.
The extendedErrCode method of the ooSQLiteConnection class does the same for a connection object.
See the example of oosqlErrCode.

section.title: oosqlExtendedResultCodes
section.para: Does nothing: extended result codes are always enabled in ooSQLite.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
db [required]
A handle to a database connection. It is not used.
onOff [required]
True or false. It is not used.
Returns OK.
The routine is provided for completeness, so that programs written for the SQLite API can be translated directly.
In SQLite, the sqlite3_extended_result_codes API enables or disables extended result codes. ooSQLite enables them when it opens a connection, and they can not be disabled.
The extendedResultCodes method of the ooSQLiteConnection class does the same for a connection object.

section.title: oosqlFinalize
section.para: Deletes a prepared statement and releases the resources it uses.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
stmt [required]
The handle to a statement prepared by oosqlPrepare. The handle can be null; then this routine does nothing.

Returns OK if the last execution of the statement had no error, if it was never executed, or if the handle is null. If the last oosqlStep failed, the error code it returned is returned again. In all cases, the statement is finalized.

Every statement prepared without error must be finalized once, and only once. After oosqlFinalize, the handle is not valid any more: it must not be used in any routine, and it must not be finalized again. ooSQLite can not detect this, and the result is unpredictable; the interpreter can crash. Dropping the variable that holds the handle, as the example does, prevents using it by mistake.

All the statements of a connection should be finalized before the connection is closed: while there is any statement that is not finalized, oosqlClose returns BUSY and the connection stays open. Unlike a statement object of the object orientated interface, a statement handle is never finalized automatically.
The functionality of the oosqlFinalize routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_finalize API.
The finalize method of the ooSQLiteStmt class does the same for a statement object.

This example executes an INSERT that fails, because the table already has a row with that id, and then finalizes the statement, which returns the same error code again:
rc = oosqlPrepare(db, "INSERT INTO foods(id, name) VALUES(1, 'Toast');", 'stmt') rc = oosqlStep(stmt) say rc oosqlErrMsg(db) say oosqlFinalize(stmt) drop stmt /* Output: 1555 UNIQUE constraint failed: foods.id 1555 */
